74090218.title: 2009_NFC_Wild_Card_playoff_game_(Green_Bay–Arizona)
74090218.extract:
### Background

#### Green Bay Packers
The 2009 Green Bay Packers finished the regular season with an 11–5 record, placing second in the NFC North division behind the 12–4 Minnesota Vikings. Under head coach Mike McCarthy, the team scored a franchise-record 461 points, ranking third in the NFL, while allowing 297 points on defense, good for sixth in the league. Quarterback Aaron Rodgers, in his second full season as starter after replacing Brett Favre, threw for 4,434 yards, 30 touchdowns, and seven interceptions during the regular season. The Packers' offense was bolstered by running back Ryan Grant, who rushed for 1,253 yards, and a receiving corps led by Donald Driver and Greg Jennings. Defensively, the unit featured players like cornerback Charles Woodson, who won the NFL Defensive Player of the Year award with nine interceptions. Green Bay started the season 4–4 but won seven of their final eight games to secure the NFC's fifth playoff seed. The team's turnaround from a 6–10 record in 2008 was attributed to improved offensive line play and defensive adjustments.

#### Arizona Cardinals
The 2009 Arizona Cardinals compiled a 10–6 record to win the NFC West division for the second consecutive year, under head coach Ken Whisenhunt. The team scored 375 points (11th in the NFL) and allowed 325 (14th). Quarterback Kurt Warner, at age 38, led the offense with 3,753 passing yards, 26 touchdowns, and 14 interceptions in 15 games. Running back Beanie Wells, a rookie, contributed 793 rushing yards, while wide receivers Larry Fitzgerald and Anquan Boldin (though Boldin was limited by injuries) formed a strong passing attack. The Cardinals' defense ranked 20th in yards allowed but forced 25 turnovers. Arizona started 1–2 but won nine of their next 13 games before resting players in the finale. As defending NFC champions from the 2008 season, where they lost Super Bowl XLIII to the Pittsburgh Steelers, the Cardinals earned the NFC's fourth seed and home-field advantage for the Wild Card round.

#### Regular-season meeting
The Packers and Cardinals met in Week 17 of the regular season on January 3, 2010, at University of Phoenix Stadium, with Green Bay winning 33–7. Arizona, having already clinched the NFC West, rested several starters, including Warner for most of the game and limiting Fitzgerald's snaps. Rodgers threw for 235 yards and one touchdown, while the Packers' defense intercepted three passes, including a 45-yard return for a touchdown by Woodson. Matt Leinart started at quarterback for Arizona, completing 13 of 21 passes for 96 yards and two interceptions. The lopsided result provided little predictive value for the playoff rematch, as Cardinals players later noted the rest allowed them to enter the postseason healthier.

### Broadcasting
The game was televised nationally by Fox, with Joe Buck providing play-by-play commentary, Troy Aikman as color analyst, and Pam Oliver on sideline reporting. It drew an average viewership of approximately 30 million, reflecting interest in the quarterback matchup and the teams' recent playoff histories.

### Game summary
The game kicked off at 2:40 p.m. MST, with an attendance of 61,926 in the indoor University of Phoenix Stadium. Arizona won the coin toss and elected to receive.

#### First quarter
Arizona dominated early, scoring on their first three possessions. After a Green Bay three-and-out, the Cardinals drove 80 yards in seven plays, ending with a 1-yard touchdown run by Tim Hightower. On the ensuing kickoff, Packers returner Jordy Nelson fumbled, leading to a 15-yard touchdown pass from Warner to Early Doucet. Later, after intercepting Rodgers, Arizona added a 23-yard field goal by Neil Rackers to lead 17–0.

#### Second quarter
Green Bay responded with an 83-yard drive, capped by a 1-yard touchdown run by Rodgers. Arizona extended their lead to 24–7 with another 15-yard Warner-to-Doucet touchdown pass. The Packers added a 20-yard field goal by Mason Crosby as time expired, making the halftime score 24–10.

#### Third quarter
Arizona opened with a 33-yard touchdown pass from Warner to Fitzgerald, pushing the lead to 31–10. Green Bay rallied with a 6-yard touchdown pass from Rodgers to Jennings and an 11-yard pass to Nelson, narrowing it to 31–24. The Cardinals answered with an 11-yard Warner-to-Fitzgerald touchdown, leading 38–24 at quarter's end.

#### Fourth quarter
The Packers tied the game with a 30-yard touchdown pass from Rodgers to James Jones and a 1-yard run by John Kuhn. Arizona regained the lead at 45–38 with a 17-yard Warner-to-Steve Breaston touchdown. Green Bay forced overtime with an 11-yard touchdown pass from Rodgers to Spencer Havner with 1:52 remaining. Arizona drove into field-goal range, but Rackers missed a 34-yard attempt wide left as regulation ended.

#### Overtime
Green Bay won the overtime coin toss and received. On the third play, Rodgers was sacked by Michael Adams, fumbling the ball, which Dansby recovered and returned 17 yards for the winning touchdown. The play was reviewed but upheld, as officials ruled no face-mask penalty occurred.

### Statistics

| Statistic | Green Bay Packers | Arizona Cardinals |
|-----------|-------------------|-------------------|
| First downs | 24 | 26 |
| Total yards | 493 | 531 |
| Rushing yards | 89 | 156 |
| Passing yards | 404 | 375 |
| Turnovers | 2 | 1 |
| Time of possession | 28:52 | 32:17 |

**Passing** 
- Green Bay: Aaron Rodgers – 28/42, 423 yards, 4 TD, 1 INT 
- Arizona: Kurt Warner – 29/33, 379 yards, 5 TD, 0 INT 

**Rushing** 
- Green Bay: Ryan Grant – 11 carries, 64 yards 
- Arizona: Beanie Wells – 14 carries, 91 yards 

**Receiving** 
- Green Bay: Jermichael Finley – 6 receptions, 159 yards 
- Arizona: Steve Breaston – 7 receptions, 125 yards, 1 TD 

The game set NFL playoff records for combined points (96), combined touchdowns (13), and combined passing yards (802). Warner's five touchdowns with four incompletions marked a rare efficiency milestone.

### Aftermath
Arizona advanced to the NFC Divisional playoffs, facing the top-seeded New Orleans Saints on January 16, 2010, where they lost 45–14. Warner, who suffered a concussion in that game, announced his retirement on January 29, 2010, ending a 12-year career that included two MVP awards and a Super Bowl win. The Cardinals' playoff run highlighted their offensive prowess but exposed defensive inconsistencies, leading to a 5–11 record in 2010. 

For Green Bay, the loss ended their season but spurred improvements; the Packers won Super Bowl XLV the following year with a similar core. The game underscored Rodgers' potential, as he set a franchise playoff record for passing yards. Both teams' performances contributed to discussions on NFL playoff formats, particularly regarding division winners hosting higher-seeded wild-card teams.
